Yes — we should rebuild the Brazil plan for the July through September sign ups drop scenario and the accompanying spend uplift. The main reason is that a sign ups decline would push arrivals_scenario lower and cascade into reduced served_scenario and scenario.avg_active_scenario, with uplift_value_scenario also moving to a lower level.

Operationally, update plan inputs to the new scenario by aligning hires, costs, and capacity to the corresponding scenario values: set hires to {{{{Brazil.hires_scenario}}}}, keep service rate at {{{{scenario.service_rate_scenario}}}}, and align total_cost_scenario to {{{{scenario.total_cost_scenario}}}} while the uplift_value_scenario moves to {{{{scenario.uplift_value_scenario}}}}; maintain capacity per agent at {{{{rules.capacity_per_agent}}}} and support days at {{{{rules.support_days}}}}.

Germany needs {{{{Germany.end_agents}}}} agents in March to maintain the planned headcount level and service coverage. The end_agents figure represents the projected headcount required to support current activity and meet the 98 percent service floor under the plan, given the rule that each agent handles up to 10 capacity units and the current utilization. Practical point: there were no hires in March (hires_month_3 = 0), so you’d be maintaining the existing plan unless adjustments are approved.

The UAE has the most volatile demand. The main reason is that its top monthly volatility is the highest, at {{{{insight.top_monthly_cv}}}}. Day-to-day noise is high everywhere, so build in flexible capacity and look to monthly volatility patterns for planning limits; keep the focus on monthly CV when sizing teams and budgets, and adjust forecasts accordingly.
